query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Resistance of high-entropy-alloy (HEA) multilayer protective coatings to time-dependent plastic deformation is governed primarily by the extremely high density of chemically and elastically highly-misfitting interfaces. These interfaces (structural mediator) suppress dislocation climb–controlled creep because (i) they act as strong, non-coarsening sinks that annihilate and pin lattice dislocations and (ii) they block short-circuit diffusion paths. As a result, the rate-controlling mechanism switches from low-activation‐energy grain-boundary diffusion to a higher-activation‐energy lattice diffusion process, reducing steady-state creep rates by at least an order of magnitude compared with a composition-equivalent single-layer (monolithic) HEA film.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited nanolaminate coating consisting of alternating ~5–20 nm thick layers of two equiatomic refractory HEAs (e.g., NbMoTaW/VNbMoTa). Average columnar grain size ≳100 nm so that most interfaces are layer interfaces, not grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Replace the multilayer architecture with a composition-equivalent monolithic HEA film fabricated under identical sputter conditions (keeps grain size, texture, oxygen level similar) while maintaining identical overall thickness.
generation.conditions: Constant uniaxial stress σ = 0.2 σ_yield applied at 600 °C (≈0.45–0.5 T_m of the constituent elements) for 10 h in high vacuum to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Semi-coherent, chemically sharp but diffusion-misfitting interfaces spaced <20 nm apart, providing high interface density (>5×10^7 cm^−1).
generation.mechanism: Under stress and temperature, dislocation climb and grain-boundary diffusion would usually govern creep. In the multilayer, (1) large local lattice distortions and (2) elastic and chemical mismatch across each interface produce high back stress and short-range ordering that impede vacancy migration and dislocation climb. Thus the activation energy for creep approaches bulk lattice diffusion values, sharply lowering strain-rate at a given temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The steady-state creep rate of the multilayer will be ≥10× lower than that of the monolithic HEA film under identical stress and temperature. Activation energy extracted from Arrhenius plots will be at least 1.5× higher for the multilayer. TEM after creep will show high dislocation density localized at interfaces with little climb, whereas the monolith will show extensive climb and subgrain formation.
generation.baseline: Monolithic HEA film of the same overall composition and thickness but without internal layering (i.e., no periodic interfaces).
generation.boundary: Effect persists while layer thickness <~50 nm, temperature below onset of significant interdiffusion/roughening (<0.6 T_m). If annealing coarsens or eliminates interfaces, or if testing is done at much higher temperatures where interface diffusion activates, the benefit diminishes.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of the rate reduction depends on exact layer thickness, interface coherency, and residual stresses; activation energies may overlap if oxygen contamination or grain-boundary segregation dominates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings on identical substrates: (A) multilayer HEA/NHEA film with 10 nm period, 2 µm total thickness; (B) single-layer HEA film, same composition and thickness. Perform constant-load tensile creep tests at 500 °C, 550 °C, 600 °C, 650 °C, measuring strain vs. time for ≥10 h. Post-mortem TEM to examine dislocation structures and interface stability.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate (ε̇_ss) at each temperature
Activation energy Q from ln ε̇_ss vs 1/T
TEM characterization of dislocation density and interface integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If ε̇_ss(multilayer) is not at least a factor of 3 lower than ε̇_ss(monolithic) at any temperature, or if the extracted activation energies differ by <20 %, or TEM shows similar dislocation climb structures in both samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
